newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian poll will elect rubber-stamp parliament.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian poll will elect rubber-stamp parliament.

text.p: Indonesia's mostly rubber-stamp parliament will remain a body closely allied to the government after the country's general election this week despite recent glimmers of independence, political analysts said on Tuesday.

Indonesia's 125 million voters will choose 425 of the 500-member House of Representatives (DPR) when they go to the polls on Thursday. The other 75 representatives are from the military, which does not vote.
With the ruling Golkar party expected to take about 70 percent of the vote, few hold out much hope for a fresh perspective from a body maligned by critics for its passivity.

"If we see it from the vantage point as a partner in development, then we can say it is effective, but as an instrument to balance the executive it is not effective," said Mohammad Hikam, a political scientist at the Indonesian Academy of Sciences.
"It is a subordinate of the executive. Up to now, 30 years after it was created, there is not yet one bill that has been proposed by the DPR itself," Hikam told Reuters.
"The situation in Indonesia is worse than a rubber stamp as they don't even have a stamp. They just follow orders," he said.

But some political observers said in that recent years, the 11 parliamentary committees with MPs from Golkar, the minority Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) and the United Development Party (PPP) have engaged in greater scrutiny of the government.
"Ministers and government policies have come under closer scrutiny, so now I think there is a greater measure of accountability," a senior Asian diplomat said.
Hikam agreed that the committees have been more vocal in recent years, but said this was because of a few strong-willed individuals rather than any change in the system.

"The opening of the parliament's committees is more at the level of individuals and not as a committee itself. They make the committees in the DPR appear progressive, but in general I don't think it is quite happening," he said.

He noted the most high-profile of these individuals were being weeded out of the legislature, citing the case of PPP legislator Sri Bintang Pamungkas, sacked by his party with President Suharto's approval in May 1995.
Pamungkas is serving a jail sentence for defaming Suharto in a speech in Germany that same year and is now facing subversion charges for activities of his new, unrecognised political party.

Some analysts argue that the tight political controls exercised by the government on the election process and the parliament make the institution an ineffective body for channeling the aspirations of Indonesia's 200 million people.
They say that as voters choose a party rather than a person, legislators have no constituency and pledge their loyalty to the state and government rather than the people who elected them.

Soedjati Djiwandono, an analyst at Jakarta's independent Centre for Strategic and International Studies, argued in a recent newspaper column that the legislature's problem's started with the selection of candidates.

"It is even doubtful if most members of the new assembly know much about reform, recognise the need for it, know how to implement it, or have the courage to introduce the idea and initiate steps towards it," he wrote in the Jakarta Post.
"Long before the election, their candidacy was approved by the government through a special screening which makes the election a mockery of democracy," he said.

The DCA said in a statement the British CAA call for Garuda to ground its A330-300 fleet had prompted the DCA to tell Garuda its services to Hong Kong "should only be operated by aircraft other than" Trent-powered A330s.
Garuda spokesman Hartanto said the airline "always follows the standard procedure on maintenance".
"We have close contact with Rolls-Royce," he added.
